items.alt: Turbines gathered on a forested ridge

children.text: A viewpoint near Manila in Pililla, Rizal, where 27 white turbines line the hilly ridge. With Laguna de Bay and the Sierra Madre as a backdrop, it makes a half-day walking and photo trip, about
1.5~2.5 hours
away by car.
Pililla Wind Farm sits in Barangay Halayhayin in the town of Pililla, Rizal, on a hilly ridge east of Laguna de Bay. It lies about
east of central Manila as the crow flies, and its 27 white turbines stand on green hills in three groups. The turbines are Spanish-made Gamesa G90-2.0MW models, each producing
2MW
for a total of
54MW
, and they reach about
at the blade tip, roughly the height of a 33-story building. The developer, Alternergy, says the farm produces enough electricity for about 66,000 households.
There is a story behind why it ended up in Pililla. It was originally meant to be built near the
Bangui windmills
in Ilocos Norte, but the transmission lines in northern Luzon were congested, so it was moved to Rizal, closer to the Manila grid. The farm began operating in
and held its official launch on
January 19, 2016
, making it the first wind farm outside Ilocos connected to the Luzon grid. In
August 2020
, Vestas signed a five-year turbine service contract with the operator, Vena Energy.

The appeal as a destination is simple. Each turbine is enormous, and behind the ridge the lake and mountains layer one over another. According to a Reuters report, about 340,000 people visited the viewing deck after it opened to the public in

, and Alternergy advertises an average of 130,000 visitors during Holy Week, which shows how firmly it has become a weekend outing for Manila residents. It is not a theme park where you buy a ticket and go in; it is an open space where turbines stand on a village hill and you walk among them.

Honestly, there is not a lot to do here. After taking photos under the turbines, walking in the lake breeze and having a coconut juice, one or two hours is plenty. That is why many people combine it with nearby destinations in the same direction, such as the Pinto Art Museum in
Antipolo
or
Daranak Falls

in Tanay, and build a full day around them. Unlike Bangui, where the turbines stand beside the sea, this is a hill between a lake and mountains, and it can be done as a day trip from Manila. The farm was closed for a while during the
pandemic but has since reopened, and visitor reviews and photos keep appearing in
and

It suits certain travelers well. Couples and friends who like photography, families who want a scenic outing with little walking, and anyone who wants a breath of cool hilltop wind in a single day from Manila will be happy here. If you expect activities or a lot of sights, you may find it dull, and reviews say there is not much to do besides taking photos. The developer has also announced plans to extend the turbines into the neighboring mountains of Laguna province, but I could not confirm whether any expansion has actually been built. The turbines you see now number 27.

blocks.title: Walking among the turbines along the ridge

children.text: Turbines line the access road, so they stay in view as you walk. Standing close and looking up, a
tower blocks out the sky. Some areas may be closed off by fences or signs, so follow the markings.

On a clear day the surface of Laguna de Bay stretches out beyond the turbines, with hills on the far shore layered behind it. It is a scene you rarely get at other wind farms, and many people come specifically for this view.
Around

, when the sun sinks lower, golden light spreads over the grass and the turbine blades. Popular compositions include silhouettes of turbines against the backlight, or tall grass in the foreground with turbines far behind. The farm is said to close at around
, so plan to come down before dark.

blocks.title: Looking up from the foot of a turbine

children.text: Standing beneath a turbine near the viewing rest area, the white tower rises straight into the sky and a single blade is several times a person's height. If you fit the developer's logo on the nacelle and the information boards into one frame, it becomes a photo you can only take here.

Alternergy says it built a visitor center together with the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), using 18 information boards to explain wind power and the environment. Some visitors report days when the center had no staff, so treat it as something to look into only if it happens to be open.
On a privately owned hill across from the farm there is a small viewpoint that charges about
to enter, and reviews say it gives the widest view, with more than ten turbines in sight at once. There are said to be separate spots reached on foot and by car, so check on site.
Stalls near the entrance sell coconut juice (about
) and sweet pineapples grown on nearby farms, and you can buy palm-sized wooden mini turbines carved by villagers as souvenirs. Reuters reported that about 45 residents make these souvenirs.

blocks.title: A drive along the lakeside East Road

children.text: If you drive, the trip is part of the experience. Manila East Road passes through Taytay, Angono, Binangonan, Cardona, Morong, Baras and Tanay in turn, following the edge of Laguna de Bay. A short stop at a point with a lake view helps build the mood before you see the turbines.

items.title: Half-day trip by car
items.subtitle: From Manila, on a weekday morning

children.text: Leave Manila or Quezon City, pass through Antipolo and head onto Manila East Road
Pass the turn-off for the Pililla access road and arrive at the wind farm parking lot; agree on the parking fee and leave your car
Walk along the ridge, take photos beneath the turbines and look around the lake viewpoints
Have coconut juice and pineapple at the stalls, then climb the private hilltop viewpoint for the full view
Head back toward Tanay town for lunch
Go on to the Pinto Art Museum in Antipolo for the afternoon, or swim at Daranak Falls
Leave for Manila before the evening rush begins
On weekday mornings there are few visitors and the sun is not yet strong, so walking is comfortable. On weekends, holidays and during Holy Week, arrive before
to find parking easily.

items.title: Sunset photo trip
items.subtitle: Go late in the afternoon to catch the evening scenery

children.text: Leave Manila with plenty of time to avoid traffic on East Road
Arrive at the wind farm, park and walk the access road to scout turbine positions
Shoot at golden hour: grass, turbine silhouettes and the sky over the lake
Head back down to the parking lot before closing time
Have dinner in Tanay town
Head home aiming to be back in Manila

After dark the ridge road is very dim, with almost no street lights. Get through the last unpaved stretch before sunset and drive slowly on the way back at night. In the rainy season, fog can blur the scenery, so decide after checking the weather.

items.title: Day trip by public transport
items.subtitle: Using a van and a tricycle

children.text: Board a van or FX bound for Tanay Public Market at Araneta Center in Cubao or Starmall in Mandaluyong
Arrive at Tanay Public Market and negotiate a round-trip fare and waiting time with a tricycle driver at the terminal
Ride the tricycle for about
30 minutes
, then get off at the foot of the hill and walk a short uphill stretch
Stroll and take photos beneath the turbines
Ride the same tricycle back to Tanay Market
Lunch at a restaurant near the market
Take a jeepney toward Antipolo for the Pinto Art Museum and more, or return to Manila
If you agree on a round-trip fare with waiting time first, you do not have to look for a ride back separately. Sharing the tricycle with others cuts the cost per person considerably.
This is the easiest option. From Manila, take the Ortigas Avenue Extension up to Antipolo, then follow Manila East Road through Tanay into the town of Pililla. Estimates range from
1.5~2.5 hours
, and East Road traffic is the biggest variable.

Once you enter Pililla town, signs for the wind farm continue, and according to reviews the entrance and parking lot are on the left at the second fork. If you type Pililla Wind Farm into a map app, it will route you accurately.
The last stretch is a narrow, rocky uphill road. Reviews recommend an SUV or a high-clearance car, though some people have driven up in a sedan with care.
Road works have been going on at times, so check whether the dirt road is slippery after rain.

items.title: By van or FX and tricycle

children.text: Take a van or FX to Tanay Public Market (in Barangay Sampaloc) from places such as Araneta Center in Cubao or Starmall in Mandaluyong. The ride takes about
1 hour 20 minutes~1 hour 30 minutes
and the fare is about
From the tricycle terminal beside the market, the wind farm takes about
30 minutes
. Reviews mix reports of about
one way and
round trip, so negotiate the round trip and waiting time together.
Tricycles go only to the foot of the hill, and from there you walk up a short slope.

You can go straight from Manila by taxi or Grab, but it is hard to find a ride back, so agree on a round-trip waiting fare in advance. The exact fare varies greatly with the time of day and traffic, so confirm it with the driver beforehand. Because part of the road is unpaved, a driver may be reluctant to go up; you could also ride only as far as Tanay town and switch to a tricycle.
It is about
40km
from Antipolo to the town of Pililla and about
57km

to Manila. If you are staying in Antipolo or Tanay, the simplest way is to take a jeepney or van to Tanay Public Market and then a tricycle. For travel from Antipolo, also check the transport information in the
Antipolo
page.
Pililla Wind Farm feels very different from season to season. From
November-March

, when the northeast monsoon amihan blows, the weather is cool and clear, the lake and mountain ranges stand out sharply, and the turbines catch the wind and spin actively. One guide explains that the turbines were placed to catch the amihan wind. Even midday is fairly comfortable, so this is the best time for walking.
From
April-May
the dry season continues, but the hill has almost no shade, so the midday sun is fierce. Go early in the morning or around dusk. From
June-October
the southwest monsoon habagat brings frequent rain, the dirt road turns muddy and fog can set in. From
August-October
typhoons may pass through, so check the forecast and avoid days of heavy rain.
If you want a quiet day, choose a weekday morning. On weekends, holidays and during Holy Week, crowds make parking hard to find.

items.note: Many reports say there is no set entrance ticket at the entrance; follow on-site notices

items.label: Parking (car)
items.note: Per car; common in 2025-2026 reviews, but some say it is free, so confirm on site

items.label: Tricycle (Tanay-farm)
items.note: Per round trip for one tricycle; some say ₱300 one way, so negotiate; split among passengers

items.label: Lunch
items.note: Per person at a restaurant in Tanay town

children.text: Prices are rough estimates for
and may change depending on local conditions.

Pililla Wind Farm is a half-day trip, so an overnight stay is not necessary. If you want to stay a night, Tanay town and Antipolo have many resorts and campsites, and Altitude & Coolwinds, a private facility at the entrance to the farm, is described as offering a viewing deck, parking, hut rental and lodging. Contact them directly about prices and whether they are open before you visit.

There are stalls and small souvenir shops at the entrance where you can buy coconut juice (buko juice), local pineapples and wooden turbines. For a proper meal, most people come back down to Tanay town. Grilled tilapia, dalag (snakehead) and hito (catfish) from Laguna de Bay are introduced as local specialties and can be tried at lakeside restaurants. The turbine area has almost no shade or restaurants, so it is best to bring a simple lunch box or snacks.
Bring plenty of cash. Parking, restrooms, the private viewpoint and the stalls mostly accept cash only, and there is no ATM on site. Small bills of
and
are useful.
On weekdays
is the quietest, and
is good for sunset photos. On weekends and during Holy Week, arrive before
There is almost no shade on the hill. Bring a hat, sunglasses, sunscreen and water, and a light jacket is helpful for windy days.
Wear sneakers or trekking sandals. The last stretch is an unpaved uphill, and it is slippery after rain.
When you park, ask about the fee first and get a receipt or ticket if possible. Reports are mixed between free and about
, so it is safest to check the notice on site.

There is no published official rule for drones. If you want to fly one, use it only in open areas far from turbines and power lines, and ask the farm's security or the barangay office first for any commercial shoot.
Mobile signal can get weak, so download an offline map and tell someone your plans.

There is no shade and hardly anywhere to sit. If you want to rest on the grass, bring a mat or a thin blanket, and a wide-angle lens or your phone's wide-angle mode is good for capturing the turbines and the lake together.
Take your trash back with you. Smoking is not allowed on the grounds, and there are notices telling visitors to stay away from cliff edges.

The farm's operating rules are not detailed on an official site, so fees and hours differ from review to review. Check recent reviews and the notices from the Pililla town tourism office and the developer before you go.
Entrance and parking fees differ between reviews. Some say it is free and some report about
for a car, so if you are asked for an amount that is not fixed, check the rate card and ask for a receipt.
The farm was closed to the public during the
pandemic, and some reviews still describe it as closed for a while. Visit records continue now, but access may be restricted for maintenance, events or disasters.
Lightning and strong wind are dangerous on a hilltop. If thunder rumbles, move away from the turbines and the ridge, and stay away from cliffs and slopes.
Some areas may be off limits. Do not cross fences or safety signs, and do not go near electrical facilities or transmission towers.
The last dirt stretch can be very slippery after rain. If your car cannot get up, park below and walk up.
Restrooms are few and paid, and there is little shade or food, so with children or older people prepare water, snacks and tissue. It is hard to get around by wheelchair.
It is about
40km
from the town of Pililla, or about
1 hour~1 hour 30 minutes
by car. The Pinto Art Museum with its contemporary art, Antipolo Cathedral and hilltop restaurants with views make a good pairing with the turbines.
This family-friendly waterfall is a stop you can make on the way back toward Tanay town. Swimming in the water pouring down a mossy rock wall is a nice way to end a morning at the turbines.
A hiking destination that goes deeper into the Sierra Madre foothills beyond Tanay. It is too much to fit into the same day as the turbines, so plan it as a separate trip.
This is a classic day-trip attraction over in Laguna province, where you ride a boat up the rapids. It can take more than an hour to get there, so check road conditions and set aside a separate day.
